# Day 5 — Overview {#sec-day5}

Today is about the number you report and the model that makes it look good.
Every day so far has ended with a single score — an MAE, an accuracy — and has
asked you to take it at face value. This morning you will find out what each
of the standard scores conceals, and this afternoon you will meet the first
model in the booklet that can score perfectly on the data it was fitted to
while being worse than useless on anybody else. @sec-day1 left the loose end:
*MAE was chosen for us*. So was accuracy. Today you choose, and you defend the
choice.

The thread running through the day is a question a reviewer will ask you:

> **Compared with what?**

Every exercise answers it with something concrete: the predict-the-mean
baseline, the majority-class rule, a shuffled outcome, a model with no tuning,
and finally a logistic regression that the random forest does not beat.

## Objectives

By the end of the day you should be able to, without looking anything up:

::: {.objective-list}
- Compute RMSE, MAE and R² for a regression, and say which one answers which
  question and which one is a statement about the population rather than the
  model.
- Compute accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC for a classifier, and
  quote the majority-class accuracy next to every accuracy you report.
- Explain why a model with perfect training performance is not a good model,
  and name the one piece of evidence that distinguishes learning from
  memorising.
- Tune hyperparameters by grid search over resampled training data, and say in
  one sentence why the test set takes no part in that choice.
- Decide whether a difference between two models is larger than the
  uncertainty in the comparison.
:::

| | Exercise | Time | Mode |

| — | break | 15 min | |

: {tbl-colwidths="[6,52,18,24]"}

Do them in order. Exercises 5.2, 5.3 and 5.4 share one 70/30 stratified split
of `data/diabetes.csv`, rebuilt in the first cell of each page, so the numbers
on the three pages are directly comparable — and the comparison at the end of
5.4 is the point of the afternoon.

## What you need before you start

- R and Python working locally, and this project open in your editor
  (@sec-setup). Day 5 adds two R packages to the ones you already have:
  `rpart.plot` for drawing trees and `ranger` for the random forest. Both are
  installed by `scripts/setup_local.R`.
- @sec-classification-metrics assumes the logistic regression of
  @sec-logistic-regression and the threshold argument of @sec-thresholds.
- @sec-decision-trees and @sec-random-forest assume the leakage argument of
  @sec-leakage: a preprocessing step fitted outside the resampling loop has
  seen the rows it is about to be scored on.

::: {.callout-note}
## The data is synthetic, and the zeros are real
`data/diabetes.csv` is `mlbench`'s synthetic replacement for a dataset
withdrawn on consent grounds, and it keeps the original's defect: zeros where
zero is physiologically impossible (@sec-data-diabetes). Today's models are
fitted on those zeros without comment, which is deliberate — you handled them
on Day 2, and leaving them in means today's numbers are comparable with the
ones you produced then.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Running the day.** The two halves have different shapes. The morning is
careful reading of metrics and is best done with frequent short plenaries —
ask for the number, write it on the board, ask what is missing beside it. The
afternoon is a single argument told in two pages, and it does not work if 5.3
is rushed: the student has to personally watch a model achieve 1.000 and then
fail.

**Where the time actually goes.** Exercise 5.1 Task 2 overruns when students
re-split by hand rather than reusing the pattern; say at the start that nothing
on the page is new code. Exercise 5.3's grid search is four seconds, so the
time there goes on reading `show_best()`, which is worth protecting.

**Plenary.** Run the Day 5.4 Task 3 comparison as a vote before anyone looks:
*random forest or logistic regression?* Nearly the whole room picks the forest.
Then put R's test AUCs and Python's side by side — the two languages disagree
about the winner, by less than the standard error of either estimate. That is
the day in one slide, and it is more convincing than any amount of saying it.

**If a day has to be dropped from the module**, this is not it. Days 3 and 6
teach methods; this one teaches the habit of asking "compared with what", and
every later day assumes it.
:::
